name: Pathiri
tagline: Malabar’s thin rice pancake — an iftar and food‑trail essential
summary: Pathiri is the thin rice flour pancake of Malabar (Mappila) kitchens, central to Malappuram and Kozhikode food culture and a staple on Ramadan iftar tables and evening food trails.
description: Pathiri is a soft, thin pancake made from rice flour that sits at the heart of Mappila — North Malabar — cooking. It appears at everyday meals, wedding feasts and especially on iftar and Eid menus.
The dish matters because it shows Malabar’s long coastal links: rice‑based breads and layered/filled variants reflect Arab and local exchanges that shape the region’s taste.

For a visitor, pathiri is both a street‑food bite in evening markets and a homely plate item served with fish, chicken or mutton curries, coconut chutneys and pickles — try several varieties to appreciate the local range.
highlights: Ramadan/iftar staple across Kozhikode, Malappuram and Kannur.
Many regional varieties: ari pathiri (plain), chatti/pathiri (layered), irachi/iraichi (meat), meen (fish) and sweet types.
Serves as bread in North Malabar — pairs with spicy curries and fried or stewed fish/meat.
Found in evening markets, mosque neighbourhoods and traditional sweet/halwa shops.
Rice‑based (gluten‑free base) but some modern variants use wheat/maida — ask if you need gluten‑free.

sections.heading: Background
body: Pathiri develops from rice‑flour traditions in North Kerala and the Mappila community. Historical links with Arab traders and regional rice culture shape its forms and seasonality.

The pancake is both everyday food and ceremonial: families prepare layered or stuffed pathiris for weddings, and street stalls and home kitchens produce large quantities during Ramadan evenings and Eid celebrations.

sections.heading: Varieties and taste
body: Ari pathiri (plain, paper‑thin) is soft and neutral — a canvas for rich curries. Chatti/Chatti‑pathiri is layered like a casserole when made with fillings; irachi (meat) and meen (fish) pathiris are savoury, while some smaller fried or sweet pathiri types appear as snacks.
Textures range from paper‑thin and pliable to thicker, steamed parcels. Flavours come from the curry or stuffing it accompanies rather than from heavy spices in the pancake itself.

sections.heading: Where to try — Malabar food trails and iftar markets
body: Kozhikode and Malappuram towns host stalls and neighbourhood kitchens that specialise in pathiri. Evening markets and mosque precincts serve freshly made pathiris at iftar during Ramadan; food‑trail guides recommend visiting old markets and coastal food streets between October and March for the best variety and dry weather.
Look for small shops that sell pathiri with fish or mutton curry, halwa shops that include sweet pathiri variants, and home‑style eateries on the Malabar food trail from Kozhikode up to Kannur.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Go in the evening if you want the Ramadan market buzz and freshly made pathiris with tea or curry; outside Ramadan you still find pathiri in traditional Mappila eateries and on food trails.
If your trip targets festivals or iftar menus, confirm Ramadan/Eid dates and local market schedules before you travel — menus and evening‑market hours move with the lunar calendar and local practice.

latest.text: Feature coverage during Ramadan 2026 highlights pathiri as an iftar favourite across Malabar and traces its Arab‑influenced origins.

visitorInfo.bestTime: October–March (dry, cooler weather and peak food‑trail season; Ramadan markets appear when the lunar calendar places Ramadan here — check dates)
visitorInfo.howToReach: Reach Kozhikode (Calicut) or Malappuram/Tirur by rail or road; use local buses, autos or taxis to old markets, mosque neighbourhoods and food streets where pathiri is sold.
etiquette: Ask what the pathiri is filled or served with — plain ari pathiri is rice‑based, while irachi/meen versions contain meat or fish.
Try pathiri at evening stalls during Ramadan for the busiest, freshest experience — confirm Ramadan dates and market times before planning.
If you need gluten‑free food, confirm the pancake is rice‑only; some modern variants or fillings use wheat/maida.
Pair pathiri with a local curry (fish, chicken or mutton) or with simple coconut chutney to taste the regional balance of spice and coconut.
